messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Jorge is a 70-year-old dentist who has maintained a successful solo practice for over four decades. He presented for therapy at the urging of his daughter, reporting overwhelming anxiety and intrusive memories that have become unmanageable since his wife’s death two years ago. The origins of his distress trace back fifty years to his time as a university student in his home country. He was participating in a peaceful student protest for democratic reforms when the military was dispatched to disperse the crowd. Without warning, the soldiers opened fire. Jorge remembers the sudden, deafening crack of rifles, the chaos, and the feeling of being utterly powerless as he watched friends and classmates fall. He managed to escape physically unharmed, but the event has shadowed his entire life.

For many years, Jorge’s life in America—his marriage, his children, his meticulous work as a dentist—acted as a bulwark against the past. After his wife passed, however, the structure of his life weakened, and the memories began to intrude with a new and terrifying intensity. Now, when a memory returns, it is not a thought but a full sensory hijacking. He reports that it feels "completely real," the sterile scent of his dental office replaced by the smell of gunpowder and the quiet hum of his equipment drowned out by the remembered sounds of gunfire and screaming. The experience is so emotionally overwhelming that he has to stop what he is doing, often gripping the dental chair in his operatory until the episode passes. He finds he cannot put the event into words, the horror of it residing in a place beyond language.

This re-experiencing is now easily set off by a range of cues. The sight of any person in uniform, from a police officer to a postal worker, can trigger a jolt of panic. This has made navigating daily life a constant exercise in threat assessment. He finds himself watching other people closely, scanning their hands and faces for any sign that they might pose a danger. Upon entering any building, including his own office each morning, his first instinct is to locate all the exits. The sound of a car backfiring or even a dropped tool in the clinic can send him into a state of high alert that lasts for hours. These triggers not only activate his sense of imminent threat but also frequently plunge him directly back into the nonverbal, sensory horror of the memory itself.

In response to this constant state of fear, Jorge has developed a rigid set of behaviours he believes are necessary for his survival. He has begun carrying an old, unloaded handgun—a keepsake from his late brother—in his briefcase, convinced that he must be prepared for violence at any moment. This act of carrying a weapon, meant to increase his safety, instead primes him to see threats everywhere, sharpening his hypervigilance and making him even more sensitive to potential triggers like loud noises or authority figures. He assiduously avoids all news reports, especially those concerning political unrest or violence, fearing they will trigger another overwhelming memory. Perhaps most corrosively, he spends hours each evening lost in rumination, replaying the events of the protest and blaming himself for what happened, convinced that if he had been braver or faster, he could have saved someone. This cycle of self-blame serves only to keep the memory emotionally raw and readily accessible, ensuring that the slightest trigger can bring it rushing back with full force.

The closed loop of his experience has tightened over the past year. A trigger, like a patient mentioning their military service, reactivates the memory. The raw, sensory horror of the memory reinforces his conviction that the world is a dangerous place and that he is unsafe. This intense feeling of threat drives his coping strategies—scanning exits, avoiding the news, carrying the weapon. These strategies, in turn, amplify his sense of threat and make him more likely to notice triggers in his environment, creating a self-sustaining cycle of fear. He finally sought help after an incident last month when a patient arrived in his Army Reserve uniform, triggering a flashback so intense that Jorge had to abruptly end the appointment, retreating to his private office, shaking and unable to speak. He is terrified of losing the practice he built over a lifetime and fears he is becoming trapped permanently in the worst day of his life.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not describe how the trauma memory itself makes the patient more sensitive or aware of triggers.
The vignette does not describe how the patient's general sense of threat makes him more sensitive or aware of triggers; instead, it attributes this effect to his maladaptive strategies.
